_doc.templates_placeholders:
templates.headline_intro/headline_outro deliberately mix two placeholder syntaxes, each owned by a different substitution pass: single-brace `{name}` is resolved ONCE, at config-merge time, from the country's own headline_name (frontend/src/data.js's mergeFocusConfig, mirrored by backend/util/focus_config.py's merge_focus_config — keep the two in sync) and is baked into the merged `headline` string shipped to the client. Double-brace `{{date}}`/`{{end}}`/`{{comb}}`/`{{dir}}`/`{{pos}}`/`{{acft}}`/`{{flights_and_landings}}` are resolved on every render, from live filter/What-If state, by frontend/src/data.js's fillHeadlineStats (called via panel-data.js's interpolateHeadline and directly from map.js) — these must stay unresolved until then, so they use a visually distinct syntax on purpose. templates.closing has no placeholders. One other field elsewhere in this file has its own separate single-brace placeholders substituted by yet other code, not by either function above: share.country's `{pct}`/`{adjective}`/`{name}` (frontend/src/share-links.js). The tour and contact actions in the sidebar footer are real buttons, labelled from footer.tour_label and footer.contact_label — `{tour_link}`/`{contact_link}` are still substituted into footer.text if an older config string carries them, but the shipped text no longer does. footer.text's `
` tags are literal HTML line breaks, rendered via {@html}. footer.contact_url is the single source of the contact-form URL: both the frontend (ContentPanel.svelte, via getFocusConfig()) and the backend's roles_page.py read this same key rather than each hardcoding their own copy.

info.headline:
’Flyover country’ is a derogatory US term referring to states that wealthier Americans fly over but don’t think or care about - as they move between destinations they consider more important.

Is your country… a flyover country? You may have a choice.

The US-Israeli war on Iran and Lebanon is completely reliant on transatlantic flights crossing Europe, as well as resupply routes connecting the war theater to bases in Germany and the UK.

Many countries on the way could decide which planes to let into their airspace - ones that help Ukraine or European interests, or ones that counter them.

Are your leaders giving speeches but not doing what’s in their power?

sections.text: This site combines two kinds of content. The map, the routes, and the percentage figures in each country's headline are computed from tracked flight data. The surrounding text — the framing questions, the calls to action, and the judgments about what individual countries should do — is this project's own commentary, not a measurement. The tier labels used for countries ('Blocks most overflight (long-standing)', 'Acted in 2026 to block some overflight', 'Permits most overflight') are an editorial classification based on the sourced per-country research, not an automated score. See Methodology, in the Info list, for how the data is computed and how tiers are assigned.
sections.title: How to read this page

sections.text: Without European cooperation, the US cannot sustain its war on Iran. Every major air route from the continental US or its main European bases in the UK and Germany to the Middle East theater crosses European airspace.
sections.title: The war depends on European airspace

sections.text: Spain, France, Switzerland and Austria deny overflight to planes involved in offensive operations in this war, as well as to ones resupplying the Israeli war effort. At the same time, Ukrainian and Russian airspace are effectively closed to US military aircraft.
sections.title: Some countries already say no

sections.text:
Consequently, the majority of US military flights connecting the US or its main European supply bases in the UK or Germany to the war theater follow a single route, with multiple single points of failure.

If Slovakia or Hungary were to similarly deny overflight, US operations could be severely disrupted. Other countries are in slightly less strong positions for unilateral action, but can still block the route together, or apply significant pressure unilaterally.
sections.title: A single country could end the war

sections.text:
On Tuesday, May 5, Saudi Arabia and Kuwait told the United States it could not use their airspace or bases for a planned offensive. The US stopped the offensive and only resumed two days later after both countries reversed course and permitted overflight. If they can stop the war, maybe you can too.

Note: this event took place after 16 April 2026, when the flight data mapped on this site ends, so it is not reflected in the map, routes, or percentages elsewhere on this page.
sections.title: It has already worked

sections.text:
Europeans could stop this war today. It is unjust and illegal, and hurts countless people in West Asia. But it also damages European interests, both economically and by distracting from Ukraine.

Click on the various countries to see the routes through them, and explore the data.
sections.title: What can your country do?

sections.text: US military flights in Europe also assist in repelling Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The US' use of European airspace and bases for another illegal and unjust aggressive war has strained transatlantic cooperation. It has reduced resources available to the Ukrainian war effort, and it has undermined allied countries' reputation and standing by making European countries complicit in war crimes and violations of international law.  It has also hurt European economies and residents.  You have a choice about which planes you let in.  Use your judgment.
sections.title: What about Ukraine?

message: European countries have a choice about when US military planes enter their airspace, and on what missions. The current war against Iran is hurting your own people. You can condition your cooperation. Can you stop this war?
